newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Fighting inflation main policy - Morocco C.Bank head.
newsitem.headline: Fighting inflation main policy - Morocco C.Bank head.

text.p: Moroccan central bank governor said on Tuesday that the main plank of Rabat's monetary policy was to battle inflation and ensure "stability of the national currency (dirham), both internally and externally."

Governor Mohamed Seqat of the Bank al-Maghrib (central bank) made his remarks in a speech to a meeting on "strategy to face the challenge of a European Union-Moroccan free trade zone" being introduced by the year 2010:
"The monetary policy in Morocco is centred on stability of prices. This is not an end in itself but rather the means the monetary authorities have to promote conditions for a more productive economy.

"This is for the simple reason that economic agents, households or businesses, can take the best decisions on saving and investing when they are convinced the future value of their savings or their investment will not be eroded by inflation."
Morocco's annual inflation fell to 3.0 percent last December from 6.1 percent in the year 1995.
Finance Minister Mohamed Kabbaj has said savings are relatively weak at 18 to 20 percent of Gross Domestic Product and he is working on plans to raise it to 25 percent.
Seqat said monetary policy had to be flexible, tightening or loosening according to whether the economy produced demand pressure or a slowdown in growth.
"The inescapable objective of monetary policy will thus consist in watching to ensure sufficient financing of productive activites while avoiding reviving inflationist tensions...," he said.
Morocco and the European Union in February 1996 signed an association accord gradually to implement a free trade zone by 2010.

The governor said Morocco had started liberalising and opening up its economy early in the 1980s. Monetary control instruments had been progressively renovated to enable the central bank to regulate liquidity volumes.

"It remains however that the mastery of the public finance situation -- and from that the Treasury's recourse to bank-originated financing -- would appear indispensable for the success of such a policy.
"That would enable the generation of more resources to profit productive activity, without inflationist pressures," he said.
Seqat said Moroccan companies should "show more transparency" to be able to turn to public savings and new means of finance as alternatives to bank credit.

Since the last exchange rate adjustment to the dinar in May 1990 "the monetary authorities have given priority to seeking stability of the real external value of the national currency...This choice must remain a constant (feature) of our economic and financial policy," he added.
On budgetary policy, Seqat said lower interest rates reduced the service of public debt and helped bring down the deficit.
